cards.patriot-driver: The Patriot is the civilian version of the most famous thing Seamus has made. Matt Kuchar commissioned American flag covers for the entire 2016 U.S. Ryder Cup team, each one carrying thirteen hand-cut stripes and fifty embroidered stars, and the standing line runs on that same DNA. It is wool, cut and sewn in Beaverton and fleece-lined like everything the shop makes.
cards.glacier-driver: Megan Chisti was a womenswear designer at Pendleton Woolen Mills when she sewed the first Seamus cover, and the licensed Pendleton line closes that loop. Glacier Peaks is the Pacific Northwest blanket pattern, and in wool on a driver it is the cover Seamus customers buy more than any other.
cards.dude-driver: Seamus embroiders the Dude onto natural canvas in full Big Lebowski costume, cardigan and White Russian posture and all, and the cover has been a permanent resident of the best-sellers page. The brand plays its pop-culture references completely straight rather than winking at them, which is why they land.
cards.stogie-driver: Kramer is the Seinfeld counterpart to the Dude, caught mid-stride with a cigar and embroidered onto the same natural canvas. Between the two of them Seamus has built the best pop-culture corner in headcovers, and the covers are hand-sewn in Oregon rather than screen-printed offshore.
cards.glenaffric-driver: Glen Affric is held to be Scotland’s oldest surviving tartan, recovered as a fragment dated to roughly the sixteenth century. Seamus cuts the modern weave into a driver cover and lines it in fleece. A four-hundred-year-old pattern stretched over a titanium head is the whole brand in one object.
cards.earlst-driver: Earl St Andrews is the best-selling tartan in the whole Seamus program, named for the home of golf. If you only ever buy one Seamus cover, the company’s own sales data says it will probably be this one. A matching blade cover sits further down for anyone who wants the set.
cards.irish-driver: The Irish National is the green-and-gold flagship of a tartan shelf that runs all the way down to individual county patterns, with Antrim, Donegal and Tipperary all cut into covers. It is cut and sewn in Beaverton like every other cover in the line. It sells quickly enough that Seamus makes no promises about St. Patrick’s Day availability.
cards.roper-driver: The Roper reads like a boot: black Tribeca leather with western stitching running the length of the shaft, cowboy-boot construction logic applied to a driver head. Leather like this takes scuffs as improvement rather than damage, so the cover gets better the longer it rides on the bag.
cards.uso-driver: Seamus has sold at every U.S. Open since Chambers Bay in 2015, and the Shinnecock capsule is this year’s edition. The cover is washed navy with nautical signal flags run across it, a nod to the Long Island setting. This is championship merchandise made by a family-owned Oregon workshop instead of a licensing conglomerate.
cards.dude-mallet: The Dude scaled down to a mallet sits at number one on Seamus’s own best-selling-headcovers list, which says something about how many golfers want Jeff Bridges guarding a putter. After enough three-putts, a cover carrying “that’s just, like, your opinion, man” starts to feel like useful equipment.
cards.earlst-putter: The blade companion to the best-selling driver tartan uses the same Earl St Andrews weave, cut down and shaped for a heel-shafted putter. It is finished the way every Seamus cover is, with a fleece lining and the one-hand elastic opening the shop is known for.
cards.glacier-putter: Glacier Peaks turns up again on the putter shelf, because Seamus customers keep voting for it and the blanket-pattern blade cover is a best seller in its own right. The pattern is the same one that leads the driver line, and the miniature-camp-blanket effect reads strongest at blade scale.
cards.buffalo-putter: Land of the Buffalo is the other Pendleton pattern holding a place on the best-seller list, a plains motif in rust and cream laid across wool. It reads more Monument Valley than Old Course, and it is the best-looking blade cover in the Seamus range.
cards.sugarskulls-mallet: Sugar Skulls is the loudest pattern in the Pendleton license, a Día de los Muertos skull motif in full color, and Seamus sells it as a house best seller across five different cover shapes. The mallet is the shape that shows the most of the print.
cards.harristweed-putter: Harris Tweed is the only fabric in the world protected by its own act of parliament, hand-woven in the Outer Hebrides and certified with an orb stamp. Seamus imports it and cuts it into blade covers in Oregon. The navy herringbone will outlast several putters.
cards.limerick-marker: The Limerick is the top seller in the Hand Forged program, and every one is hammered rather than cast or poured. Seamus’s blacksmith works in Portland and now does roughly ninety per cent of his business with the brand. Personalization is hand-stamped up to five characters and costs nothing.
cards.drainit-marker: The marker says exactly what you are supposed to do next, and it is hammered into steel by hand in the Portland smithy. Every forged piece comes out a little different from the last, which is the point of the Hand Forged line. Yours will not match anyone else’s.
cards.sugarskulls-marker: Licensed Pendleton patterns and blacksmith-made markers are the two things Seamus does that nobody else does, and this is the point where they cross. The Sugar Skulls print is translated into hammered metal and finished oil-can dark, the Día de los Muertos motif carried in texture rather than in the full color it gets on wool.
cards.horseshoe-marker: Seamus keeps a whole category of superstition markers, which is not something any other brand has thought to do, and the horseshoe is the best seller in it. It is hand-hammered steel, sized to carry to the first tee instead of hanging over a door.
cards.markit8-marker: The Mark It 8 marker completes the Lebowski set that the Dude cover and mallet begin, this one hammered in copper rather than steel. It is made for anyone who has ever wanted to mark it eight on a scorecard where an eight would be the generous number, which at $36 is a cheap enough joke to carry in a pocket.
cards.goat-tag: The bag tag is hammered steel in the shape of the Seamus goat-caddie mark, and it doubles as a bottle opener. It comes out of the same Portland smithy as the markers, one piece at a time. It hangs on the bag looking decorative until roughly the ninth hole, at which point $76 starts to look well spent.
cards.canyonlands-towel: Canyonlands is the Pendleton desert geometric woven as a jacquard towel, which puts the pattern into the cloth rather than printing it on top. The towel line keeps landing on the Seamus best-seller list. At $45 it is the cheapest way to get one of the blanket patterns onto a bag.
cards.dude-shirt: Seamus makes a shirt, and it is one of their best sellers. The Walter Sobchak line runs across a camp-collar print covered in Dude iconography, which is a lot of joke to hang on one garment. It is still funny on the eighth wear, which is more than most novelty golf shirts manage.

kickers.1: Driver and fairway covers are the engine of the company, cut and sewn in the Beaverton workshop in wool, leather, canvas and seersucker. Their site also runs a Customizer that builds one-offs out of panels, fasteners and linings.
kickers.2: The putter shelf is where the fabric library shows off: parliament-protected Harris Tweed, registered Irish tartans, Hawaiian barkcloth and licensed Pendleton patterns, fleece-lined and shaped for blades and mallets. It sits closest to the covers Megan Chisti first sewed in the garage.
kickers.3: The other half of the workshop runs on metal and cloth: markers hammered by an actual blacksmith in Portland, a bottle-opener bag tag, Pendleton towels and one very quotable shirt. Personalization on the forged pieces is hand-stamped in-house and free.
